concepts_in_source_text_not_in_dataset: מַחֲשָׁבָה (machshava — thought; the central concept of the entire Torah; declared to have immense power to actualize anything, including the experience of death itself; the source of the teaching's primary claim)

מְסִירַת נֶפֶשׁ (mesirat nefesh — self-sacrifice / martyrdom; the specific spiritual act in which thought-power is most dramatically demonstrated; accepting one's own death in thought for the sanctification of God's name)
קִידּוּשׁ הַשֵּׁם (kiddush Hashem — sanctification of God's name; the purpose and destination of מסירת נפש; the act in which the martyr's death is dedicated)

צַעַר הַמִּיתָה (tza'ar ha-mita — the pain of death; the physical sensation experienced through thought alone when accepting martyrdom; declared explicitly equivalent to actual death — 'אֵין הֶפְרֵשׁ בֵּין הַמִּיתָה בְּפֹעַל לְהַצַּעַר שֶׁמַּרְגִּישׁ מֵהַמִּיתָה בְּמַחֲשָׁבָה')
מִיתָה בְּפֹעַל (mita b'fo'al — actual death; equated with the pain experienced through thought-martyrdom; neither produces the other — they are declared the same experience: 'אֵין הֶפְרֵשׁ')

אַרְבַּע מִיתוֹת בֵּית דִּין (arba mitot beit din — the four court-imposed deaths: stoning, burning, beheading, strangling; Rabbi Akiva accepted these upon himself during the recitation of Shema; equated with מסירת נפש in this context)

קְרִיאַת שְׁמַע (kriat Shema — the recitation of Shema; the specific prayer context in which Rabbi Akiva accepted martyrdom and felt the actual pain of death; presented as the formal vehicle and bechina of מסירת נפש)

רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא (Rabbi Akiva — the paradigmatic martyr; his saying in Berakhot 61 ('all my days I was troubled — when will this come to my hand that I can fulfill it') is the proof-text for the entire teaching; he is the human embodiment of thought-martyrdom identity)

בִּטּוּל כָּל הַהַרְגָּשׁוֹת (bitul kol ha-hargashot — the nullification of all sensations/feelings; the prerequisite condition for thought to reach full potency; stated as: 'רַק שֶׁהַמַּחֲשָׁבָה תִּהְיֶה בְּבִטּוּל כָּל הַהַרְגָּשׁוֹת' — thought must operate in the nullification of all other feelings)

מָמוֹן (mamon — money/wealth; the mundane example the Rebbe gives for thought-power: 'even if one strengthens thought greatly that one will have money, one will certainly have it'; illustrates that the principle is universal, not limited to the holy domain)

analysis_notes.source_text_summary: Torah #193 is a six-line teaching about the power of thought (מחשבה). It opens with the principle that thought, if sufficiently intensified, can actualize any matter — including material wealth. The key illustration is the experience of martyrdom: one can strengthen thought so completely that when one mentally accepts dying for the sanctification of God's name (מסירת נפש על קידוש השם), one actually feels the pain of that death. The Rebbe proves this from the Talmud (Berakhot 61): Rabbi Akiva's statement 'all my days I was troubled, when will this come to my hand' is interpreted to mean that every time Rabbi Akiva recited Shema and accepted upon himself the four court-decreed deaths, his thought was so powerful that he actually felt the pain of being stoned and burned — no differently than if it were happening physically. The teaching closes with a practical warning: because thought-pain is identical to actual death-pain, one must withdraw from the meditation before the soul actually departs — otherwise one risks dying prematurely. The Torah's central bechina is: מיתה בפועל ↔ צער המיתה במחשבה — actual death and thought-death are the same. Its eitza structure: מחשבה תקיפה → מסירת נפש → מרגיש יסורי המיתה ממש.
